highlights.text: cooking or ripening something thoroughly
meat thoroughly roasted, done by heating stones and placing them over it until fully cooked
core meaning is "inclining" or "leaning" (al-mayl)
al-ḥanīf is one who inclines toward "the upright religion" (al-dīn al-mustaqīm)
glossed variously as the devotee/worshipper (nāsik), the circumcised one (makhtūn), and the one upright in his way (mustaqīm al-ṭarīqa)
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's own note: later extended readings

highlights.text: حناجر (ḥanājir) is the plural of حَنْجَرَة (ḥanjarah), "the throat."
the throat as the seat where suppressed emotion is held in
a single root built around one bodily organ, with every other sense derived from it by analogy
istiʾṣāl, the utter uprooting or wiping-out of something
"I will lead all of them astray, the way something is completely uprooted, except a few."
tender concern and softness, which may be accompanied by a sound of pain
al-ḥanān is mercy, as in "and tenderness from Us" (Q 19:13)
as in Ṭarafa's plea: "Abū Mundhir, you have destroyed; spare some of us. ḥanānayka!
he cites the report of the palm-trunk that the Messenger of God used to lean on, which "yearned" when a pulpit was made for him and he stopped leaning on it
sin (al-ithm) and culpable strain/constraint (al-ḥaraj)
ḥanitha fulānun fī kadhā means he committed a sin in such-and-such a matter
al-ḥinth fī l-yamīn is going back on / violating a sworn oath
the ḥadīth that the Prophet used to go to the cave of Ḥirāʾ and "yataḥannathu" (devote himself in worship) there for a number of nights
withholding or holding something back
A ḥuqb specifically is eighty years, plural aḥqāb
A cited verse describes a creature as "ḥaqbāʾ, piebald, [standing] on slippery ground."
the leaning or curving/crookedness of a thing
a curved sand dune is called ḥiqf (plural: aḥqāf)
a verse describing crossing an encampment and coming upon "the hollow of a low sandy tract possessing curving dunes (dhī ḥiqāfin), piled up."
a report describes passing "a gazelle ḥāqif in the shade of a tree" — i.e. a gazelle curled up, bent over, asleep
Al-ḥaqq, the opposite of falsehood, is its core, and he says every derived branch can be traced back to it by careful derivation
Ḥaqqa al-shayʾ: the thing became binding, necessary
On ḥaqīqun ʿalā in the story of Moses (Q 7:105), one scholar explains it as "binding upon me."
with Q 39:71 (al-Zumar 71) cited for the verb: "the word of punishment has come true (ḥaqqat) against the disbelievers."
al-Aʿshā: "you are surely bound (la-maḥqūqatun) to answer his call."
In a ḥadīth of ʿAlī, "when women reach naṣṣ al-ḥiqāq, the paternal kin are more entitled"
Ibn Fāris identifies two distinct original senses
someone on the brink of ruin, at death's door
The causative verb ḥarraḍa, "to urge/incite someone to do something"
Cited half-line from al-Ṭirimmāḥ: "protectors of the unarmed, worthless ones (al-aḥrāḍ)."
Al-Zajjāj's explanation of the logic: if the one urged disobeys, ruin results
two families of meaning — physical tearing/abrasion, and intense desire
ḥaraṣa ʿalayhi (also the weaker variant ḥariṣa) — he desired it intensely, greedily, hankered after it, coveted it, desired it excessively
ḥarīṣun ʿalaykum: Lane reports it as either "vehemently desirous of benefiting you" or "excessively solicitous and compassionate toward you."
aḥraṣa l-nāsi ʿalā ḥayāh: "the most vehement of men in desire for life."
Abū Dhuʾayb, using ḥaraṣtu with bi-: "Verily I had purposed to defend them by repelling aggression from them; but when death came, it was not to be repelled"
The Miṣbāḥ narrows this to blameworthy desire for worldly good
highlights.note: the Miṣbāḥ, a later moralizing gloss

highlights.text: three unrelated roots, plus one anomalous word
he derives from al-ḥarab, meaning plunder or stripping (al-salb)
al-miḥrāb = the foremost/head place of a sitting-assembly (ṣadr al-majlis)
Mistress of a miḥrāb — when I came to her, I could not reach her unless I climbed a ladder
Ibn Fāris derives three distinct senses from ḥ-r-d
He cites the Qur'an: "and they went out early, over a ḥard, able/determined" (Q68:25)
Cited in poetry by al-Ṭirimmāḥ ("Ibn Salmā was in anger")
Jarīr's line — "we build our tents facing the enemy, we seek no one's protection, nor do we dwell apart"
three basic ideas: (1) the edge or limit of a thing, (2) turning aside, and (3) gauging or measuring a thing
Qur'anic citation: "and among people is one who serves God upon a ḥarf" (22:11) — Ibn Fāris glosses this as "upon a single side."
taḥrīf of speech: deflecting words from their proper direction. Qur'anic citation: "they shift the words from their places" (4:46)
inḥarafa ʿanhu (VII) = to turn away from something
**a thing gathering densely together, and thence narrowness/tightness.**
**ḥaraj = constriction / tightness** — the abstract of the same image — and, relatedly, **sin (ithm)**.
He cites Qurʾān al-Anʿām 125: God makes the misguided one's "breast tight and constricted (ḍayyiqan ḥarajan)."
shāhid from Jaḥdar, contending "over the shares"
Hence aḥrajahā bi-taṭlīqah = he made a wife unlawful to himself by a divorce pronouncement
al-ḥarakah ("motion, movement") — defined as the direct opposite of al-sukūn ("stillness, being at rest")
Ibn Fāris holds that the three letters trace to a single origin — prevention/prohibition (manʿ)
al-ḥarām is the opposite of al-ḥalāl (the permitted)
conversely ḥarima (yaḥramu ḥaraman) is to fail to win — the same logic of being denied what one coveted
The two Sanctuaries (al-Ḥaramān), Mecca and Medina, are so called for their inviolability (ḥurma)
supported by a line of al-Aʿshā, where muḥarram means "not yet worked or suppled."
ḥaramiyy, "belonging to the Ḥaram" (with a line of al-Nābigha)
ROOT ONE — rubbing one thing against another, accompanied by heat and flaring up
ROOT TWO — a part of the body
al-ḥaraq — fire; also a burn (hole) in a garment
Cited verse: "Sulaymā's in-laws passed the night in anger, grinding their teeth."
what is contrary to slavery and free of fault or deficiency
the opposite of cold
Ḥurr means free, as opposed to a slave
A day "of heat" is a hot day (yawm ḥārr)
Al-ḥarūr is the hot wind that blows by day and by night
Ṭarafa says "this, Māwiyy, is no ḥurr thing of yours,"
Ḥumayd has a dove calling sāq ḥurr "in grief and in song."
"He guarded him from calamity"; "may God keep up your protection" (ḥirāsa = guarding/protection)
A guard is a ḥāris (plurals: ḥurrās, aḥrās)
Zamakhsharī quotes Imruʾ al-Qays describing how he got past the guards (aḥrās) and a group eager to kill him
Root 1 — gathering and acquiring
Root 2 — making a thing lean or emaciated
the tillage/cultivation of crops (ḥarth al-zarʿ)
Shāhid: Qurʾān, {نِسَاؤُكُمْ حَرْثٌ لَكُمْ} "Your women are a tilth for you" (al-Baqara 223)
staying fixed at (or confined to) a given point
Al-Rāghib cites Qur'an 72:14, fa-ulāʾika taḥarraw rashadan
a line of poetry: "man, after reaching his fullness, wanes (yaḥrī)
ḥasaba = "to count, reckon" (verbal nouns ḥasb, ḥusbān)
Cited: Qur'an 55:5, "the sun and moon are by ḥusbān"
ḥisāb = "sufficient." aḥsaba / ḥassaba someone = to give him what satisfies him
aṣāba al-arḍa ḥusbān = "locusts struck the land." Qur'an 18:40, "He sends upon it a ḥusbān from the sky,"
Shāhid: a woman's verse — "we feed the tribe's child when hungry, and give him his fill (nuḥsibu-hu)
cutting something off completely, severing it at its end
the days were "consecutive, unbroken" (mutatābiʿah)
highlights.note: first explanation, matches the site's translation

highlights.text: the days were named ḥusūm because they "cut off" good/prosperity from the people they struck
highlights.note: third explanation, judged soundest by Ibn Fāris

highlights.text: Al-ḥusn is the opposite of al-qubḥ (ugliness, foulness)
Al-maḥāsin — a person's (or anything's) good qualities, the opposite of al-masāwī (faults, bad qualities)
He cites a verse addressing a woman as "O gazelle unadorned, beautiful of neck (ḥussānat al-jīd),"
